\title{Inequality and Social Contests}
\maketitle

\section{Introduction }

The relationship between inequality and status competitions remains
unclear. On one hand, status good are seen as social waste but both
empirical studies do suggest improvement of subjective welfare with
status goods. Whether status goods -that help maintain some subjective
decency in one's reference group contributes to economic action or
not is a question that is often reserved for sociology. Relying on
Weber and Goode on how consumption is social status may be linked
with economic activity, we consider the constraints of slower social
acclimatisation posed to an closed economy of firm and labour. Viewing
social networks as a constraint that firms must accommodate, we attempt
to answer how inequality may influence pressures on establishment
of social networks. 

\subsection{Closed Economy}

The model assumes a closed economy in which all income circulates
between households and firms. Drawing on a Schumpeterian view, economic
growth arises in the model from continual introductions of new or
higher-quality goods. Workers supply labour and receive wages, and
these wages constitute the basis of domestic demand. Firms use the
revenue generated from this demand - either through investment financed
by household savings - to fund innovation. Successful innovation then
produces new varieties or improves existing products, generating the
next round of income. This circular flow of wages, consumption, and
innovation creates an endogenous engine of growth: consumption completes
one innovation cycle by returning income to firms, while investment
initiates the next by financing the search for new products. In long-run
equilibrium, firms are assumed to have already chosen an optimal allocation
of resources that sustains a steady stream of innovation and revenues.

Some investments flow back to the firm and some don't. A large part
of what doesn't flow back is not waste or efficiency loss but externality
costs to the firm. Education and training costs - where firms also
participate - are different from slow acclimatisation costs that are
spent on building social networks - maintaining notions of decency
imposed by differential social norms.
